questions.q: State the formula for speed of sound in an ideal gas and name the three variables it depends on. What is the SI unit of each variable?
questions.a: The formula is \( v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} \). Variables: \( \gamma \) (dimensionless ratio of specific heats), \( P \) (pressure in Pa = N/m²), \( \rho \) (density in kg/m³). A wrong answer (e.g., saying it depends on pressure alone) reveals the student hasn't combined the ideal gas law with the formula to see the temperature dependence.

questions.q: Why does the speed of sound in air increase with temperature even though pressure also increases when air is heated in a closed container? Explain using the formula \( v = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} \).
questions.a: In a closed container, heating increases both \( P \) and \( \rho \) proportionally (since mass and volume are fixed), so \( P/\rho \) remains constant. But in the open atmosphere, heating at constant pressure reduces density \( \rho \), so \( v \) increases. A student who says "pressure increases so speed increases" misses the simultaneous density change and the open-system condition.

questions.q: Calculate the speed of sound in air at 27°C given that at 0°C it is 331 m/s. Use the relation \( v \propto \sqrt{T} \) with absolute temperature in Kelvin.
questions.a: \( T_1 = 273 \) K, \( v_1 = 331 \) m/s. \( T_2 = 300 \) K. \( v_2 = v_1 \sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}} = 331 \times \sqrt{\frac{300}{273}} = 331 \times \sqrt{1.0989} \approx 331 \times 1.048 = 347 \) m/s. A wrong answer using Celsius temperatures (e.g., \( \sqrt{27/0} \)) reveals confusion between absolute and relative temperature scales.

questions.q: Compare the speed of sound in steel (Young's modulus \( Y = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \) Pa, density \( \rho = 7800 \) kg/m³) and in air at 20°C (343 m/s). Explain why steel has a much higher speed despite its much higher density.
questions.a: \( v_{\text{steel}} = \sqrt{\frac{Y}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{2.0 \times 10^{11}}{7800}} \approx \sqrt{2.56 \times 10^7} \approx 5060 \) m/s. This is ~15 times faster than in air. The student must recognize that Young's modulus for solids is ~10⁴ times larger than bulk modulus of gases, overwhelming the density difference. A wrong answer focusing only on density reveals a misunderstanding of the dominant role of elastic modulus.

questions.q: A student claims: "Increasing humidity decreases the speed of sound because water vapour is heavier than air." Evaluate this statement and correct it.
questions.a: The statement is false. Water vapour (molar mass 18 g/mol) is lighter than dry air (average ~29 g/mol). Adding water vapour at constant temperature and pressure reduces the average molar mass, hence density \( \rho \) decreases. Since \( v \propto 1/\sqrt{\rho} \), speed increases. A student who thinks water vapour is heavier confuses liquid water density with vapour molar mass.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a smartphone and a long corridor to measure how the speed of sound changes with temperature. Outline the procedure, measurements, and how you would analyze the data.
questions.a: Use two smartphones: one emits a sharp clap (or tone), the other records. Measure time delay \( \Delta t \) over known distance \( d \). Repeat at different temperatures (early morning, noon, evening). Plot \( v = d/\Delta t \) vs \( \sqrt{T} \) (in Kelvin). Expect linear relationship. A poor answer would ignore temperature measurement, use insufficient distance (< 50 m), or not account for reaction time in manual clapping.
